Large time behavior of solutions to a cooperative model with population flux by attractive transitionThanks: This research was partially supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number 22K03379.Thanks: †{\dagger} Department of Pure and Applied Mathematics, Graduate School of Fundamental Science and Engineering, Waseda University, 3-4-1 Ohkubo, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 169-8555, Japan.Thanks: ‡{\ddagger} Department of Applied Mathematics, Waseda University, 3-4-1 Ohkubo, Shinjuku-ku, Tokyo 169-8555, Japan.Thanks: E-mail: kuto@waseda.jp

Ryuichi Kato† and Kousuke Kuto‡
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

This paper is concerned with a diffusive Lotka-Volterra cooperative model with population flux by attractive transition. We study the time-global well-posedness and the large time behavior of solutions in a case where the habitat is a bounded convex domain and random diffusion rates equal to each other. A main result shows that when the spatial dimension is less than or equal to 3, under a weaker cooperative condition, a classical solution exists globally in time if the initial data belongs to a suitable functional space. Furthermore, it is shown that if there exists a positive steady state and the equal random diffusion rate is sufficiently large, then all positive solutions asymptotically approach the positive steady state as time tends to infinity.

Key words and phrases: 
nonlinear diffusion, population model, parabolic system, global existence, absorbing set, stability
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
35A01, 35B45, 35K51, 35B35, 92D25

1. Introduction

In this paper, we are concerned with the following diffusive Lotka-Volterra cooperative model with strongly coupled nonlinear diffusion terms:

{ut=d1Δu+α∇⋅[v2∇(uv)]+u(a1−b1u+c1v),(x,t)∈Ω×(0,T),vt=d2Δv+β∇⋅[u2∇(vu)]+v(a2+b2u−c2v),(x,t)∈Ω×(0,T),∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,(x,t)∈∂Ω×(0,T),u(x,0)=u0(x)≥0,v(x,0)=v0(x)≥0,x∈Ω,\begin{cases}u_{t}=d_{1}\Delta u+\alpha\nabla\cdot\biggl[v^{2}\,\nabla\biggl(\dfrac{u}{v}\biggr)\biggr]+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v),\ \ \ &(x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T),\\ v_{t}\,=d_{2}\Delta v+\beta\nabla\cdot\biggl[u^{2}\,\nabla\biggl(\dfrac{v}{u}\biggr)\biggr]+v(a_{2}+b_{2}u-c_{2}v),\ \ \ &(x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T),\\ \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,\ \ \ &(x,t)\in\partial\Omega\times(0,T),\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ v(x,0)=v_{0}(x)\geq 0,\ \ \ &x\in\Omega,\end{cases} (1.1)

where Ω(⊂ℝN)\Omega\,(\subset\mathbb{R}^{N}) is a bounded domain with smooth boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega, corresponding to the habitat of two species in a symbiotic relationship with each other. The unknown functions u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and v⁡(x,t)v(x,t) represent the population densities of the two species at location x∈Ωx\in\Omega and time t>0t>0. The homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions will be imposed so that each species has zero derivative in the direction of the outward unit normal vector ν\nu on the boundary ∂Ω\partial\Omega of the habitat Ω\Omega. The coefficients aia_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2) in reaction terms of the Lotka-Volterra type are real constants that can be negative, whereas bib_{i} and cic_{i} are positive constants. The coefficients aia_{i} are corresponding to the growth rate of each species, and b1b_{1} and c2c_{2} are determined from the carrying capacity of environment for each species. Here c1c_{1} and b2b_{2} represent the degree of interaction due to the symbiosis between different species. Various examples of such symbiotic pairs of species are known, e.g. the symbiotic relationship between ants and aphids is often cited. The coefficient did_{i} (i=1,2)(i=1,2) in the linear part of diffusion terms correspond to the the random diffusion rate of each individual of the species. The strongly coupled nonlinear diffusion terms ∇⋅[v2∇(u/v)]\nabla\cdot[v^{2}\nabla(u/v)] and ∇⋅[u2∇(v/u)]\nabla\cdot[u^{2}\nabla(v/u)] are expressed as in the following forms:

∇⋅[v2∇(uv)]=∇⋅(v∇u−u∇v)=vΔu−uΔv,∇⋅[u2∇(vu)]=∇⋅(u∇v−v∇u)=uΔv−vΔu.\begin{split}&\nabla\cdot\biggl[v^{2}\,\nabla\biggl(\dfrac{u}{v}\biggr)\biggr]=\nabla\cdot(v\nabla u-u\nabla v)=v\Delta u-u\Delta v,\\ &\nabla\cdot\biggl[u^{2}\,\nabla\biggl(\dfrac{v}{u}\biggr)\biggr]=\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v-v\nabla u)=u\Delta v-v\Delta u.\end{split} (1.2)

These terms describe an ecological situation where each individual of species migrates with higher probability to location with higher density of the other species. From the perspective of the diffusion process in ecology, such strongly coupled diffusion terms in (1.2) microscopically model a situation where the transition probability of each individual of each species depends on the density of the other species at the point of arrival (Okubo and Levin [14, Section 5.4]). When modeling the diffusion process of symbiotic relationship, it makes sense to set such a population flux by attractive transition to both species.

In terms of the mechanisms of ecological diffusion process, the nonlinear diffusion as in (1.2) is as typical as so-called cross-diffusion Δ⁡(u​v)\Delta(uv) and chemotaxis ∇⋅(u∇v)\nabla\cdot(u\nabla v). Actually, in the well-known monograph [14], the above three types of diffusion processes are described in parallel. In terms of partial differential equations, the cross-diffusion and the chemotaxis have been studied pure mathematically through the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto model and the Keller-Segel model, respectively, while the nonlinear diffusion as in (1.2) has not been studied pure mathematically much. In this sense, the purpose of this paper is to form the basis for mathematical prescriptions to deal with the nonlinear diffusion through the analysis of the cooperative model (1.1).

The following are studies from the viewpoint of partial differential equations for the strongly coupled nonlinear diffusion term such as (1.2): For the predator-prey model with β=0\beta=0 and b2<0b_{2}<0 in (1.1), Heihoff and Yokota [9] established the global solvability in time if N≤3N\leq 3 and derived the convergence of solutions to a positive steady state as t→∞t\to\infty with some additional conditions. For the predator-prey model, the stationary problem was also discussed by Oeda and the second author [13, 10] under homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. For (1.1) itself, Adachi and the second author [1] obtained the bifurcation structure of the non-constant positive steady states and the asymptotic behavior of the steady states as α\alpha, β→∞\beta\to\infty under a weak cooperative condition.

Based on the existing studies mentioned above, in this paper we study the solvability of (1.1). As for the time-local solvability, we can resort to the unique existence theorem for time-local classical solutions established by the series of papers by Amann [2, 3, 4, 5] that considered the solvability of a class of quasilinear parabolic equations including (1.1). Actually, by virtue of (1.2), the parabolic equations of (1.1) are represented as the following divergence form:

[utvt]=∑j=1N∂∂xj​(A⁡(u,v)​∂∂xj​[uv])+[u⁡(a1−b1​u+c1​v)v⁡(a2+b2​u−c2​v)],\biggl[\begin{array}[]{c}u_{t}\\ v_{t}\end{array}\biggr]=\sum^{N}_{j=1}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{j}}\biggl(A(u,v)\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{j}}\biggl[\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ v\end{array}\biggr]\biggr)+\biggl[\begin{array}[]{c}u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v)\\ v(a_{2}+b_{2}u-c_{2}v)\end{array}\biggr],

and all the eigenvalues of

A⁡(u,v):=[d1+α​v−α​u−β​vd2+β​u]A(u,v):=\biggl[\begin{array}[]{cc}d_{1}+\alpha v&-\alpha u\\ -\beta v&d_{2}+\beta u\end{array}\biggr]

are contained in {λ∈ℂ:Re​λ>0}\{\,\lambda\in\mathbb{C}\,:\,\mbox{Re}\,\lambda>0\,\} for any nonnegative uu and vv. Then it is possible to check all the conditions for use of [4, Theorem on p.17] to know the following unique existence of time-local classical solutions of (1.1):

Theorem 1.1 ([4]).

Assume that u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} are nonnegative functions belonging to W1,∞​(Ω)W^{1,\infty}(\Omega). Then there exist Tmax∈(0,∞]T_{{\rm max}}\in(0,\infty] and nonnegative

(u,v)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))]2(u,v)\in[\,C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{{\rm max}}))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}))\,]^{2}

which solves (1.1) classically in Ω¯×(0,Tmax)\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}). Furthermore, if Tmax<∞T_{{\rm max}}<\infty, then

lim supt↗Tmax(‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p​(Ω))=∞for all​p>N.\limsup_{t\nearrow T_{{\rm max}}}\left(\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}+\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\right)=\infty\quad\mbox{for all}\ p>N. (1.3)

Once the time-local well-posedness has been established, as in Theorem 1.1, one is naturally interested in the time-global solvability. It should be noted that concerning cooperative models such as (1.1), even in the corresponding ODE system with d1=d2=α=β=0d_{1}=d_{2}=\alpha=\beta=0, there exist solutions that blow up in finite times under the strong cooperative condition b1​c2<b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}<b_{2}c_{1}. With homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, such solutions of the ODE system are also solutions of (1.1). Then it follows that (1.1) possesses finite time blow-up solutions when b1​c2<b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}<b_{2}c_{1}. On the other hand, under the weak cooperative condition b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}, it is known that all positive solutions of the linear diffusive system with α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 are global in time and uniformly bounded ([8], [18]). It is natural to ask whether even with the strongly coupled diffusion terms as (1.2), all the classical solutions of (1.1) still exist globally in time under the same weak cooperative condition.

The first main result of this paper will show that under a weaker cooperative condition involving γ:=α/β\gamma:=\alpha/\beta (which leads to b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}), if d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and the habitat Ω\Omega is a bounded convex domain of spatial dimension 33 or less, then all classical solutions exist globally in time. Furthermore, in this case, the existence of an L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) absorbing set will be shown. From the point of view of Theorem 1.1, for any solution (u,v)(u,v), if it can be shown that ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,4​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,4​(Ω)\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,4}(\Omega)}+\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,4}(\Omega)} remains bounded for t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{{\rm max}}), the time-global solvability of the solution (i.e. Tmax=∞T_{{\rm max}}=\infty) can be obtained. In order to establish the W1,4​(Ω)W^{1,4}(\Omega) a priori estimate, we first derive the L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) a priori estimate by the comparison argument for a semilinear parabolic equation with unknown function w:=u+γ​vw:=u+\gamma v, and then, combine this L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) estimate with the maximum regularity and the energy estimate for uu and vv. For the energy estimate, we refer to ideas developed by Lou and Winkler [12] in a priori estimates of all the solutions to the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto model with equal random diffusion.

In the weak cooperative case where b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}, it is known that all positive solutions of the linear diffusive system with α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 converge to the positive steady state as t→∞t\to\infty if it exists (e.g. [18]). Under the same conditions as in the first main result, the second main result will show that if the positive constant steady state (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) exists, then it is globally asymptotically stable in the sense that all positive solutions of (1.1) asymptotically approach (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) as t→∞t\to\infty if the equal random diffusion rate d(=d1=d2)d\,(\,=d_{1}=d_{2}) is sufficiently large. The proof is based on the construction of a Lyapunov function. On the other hand, if dd is sufficiently small with the above setting, (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) can no longer be globally asymptotically stable, since the result by [1] implies the existence of nonconstant positive steady states due to the effect of the strongly coupled nonlinear diffusion terms.

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the main results. Section 3 proves the first main result, which ensures the existence of the L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) absorbing set of all positive solutions. Section 4 proves the second main result, which states the global asymptotic stability of the positive constant steady state. Section 5 discusses the relevance of the global bifurcation structure of positive steady states obtained by [1] to the behavior of the nonstationary solutions obtained in Sections 3 and 4.

2. Main results

In this section, we state main results of this paper. The first result asserts that in any convex domain Ω\Omega of space 33 dimensions or less, all the solutions guaranteed by Theorem 1.1 exist globally in time, i.e., Tmax=∞T_{{\rm max}}=\infty, with equal random diffusion rates and a weaker cooperative condition. Moreover, we also obtain the existence of an L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) absorbing set:

Theorem 2.1.

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded convex domain in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} with N≤3N\leq 3. Assume that d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and

2​γ​b1​c2>c1+γ​b2withγ=αβ.2\sqrt{\gamma b_{1}c_{2}}>c_{1}+\gamma b_{2}\quad\mbox{with}\quad\gamma=\dfrac{\alpha}{\beta}. (2.1)

If nonnegative u0u_{0} and v0v_{0} belong to W1,∞​(Ω)W^{1,\infty}(\Omega), then Tmax=∞T_{{\rm max}}=\infty in Theorem 1.1, that is, (1.1) admits a time-global solution

(u,v)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,∞))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,∞))]2.(u,v)\in[\,C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,\infty))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,\infty))\,]^{2}.

Furthermore, there exist K=K⁡(ai,bi,ci,γ)>0K=K(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i},\gamma)>0 and t0=t0​(‖u0+γ​v0‖L∞​(Ω))>0t_{0}=t_{0}(\|u_{0}+\gamma v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)})>0 such that

t≥t0⟹‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+γ​‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤K.t\geq t_{0}\ \Longrightarrow\ \|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\gamma\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq K. (2.2)

It is noted that (2.1) leads to the weak cooperative condition b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1} since c1+γ​b2≥γ​b2​c1c_{1}+\gamma b_{2}\geq\sqrt{\gamma b_{2}c_{1}}. In this sense, the condition (2.1) involving γ\gamma is an even weaker cooperative than the usual weak cooperative condition b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}.

It is easy to check that, in the weak cooperative case where b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}, (1.1) admits a unique positive constant solution

(u∗,v∗):=(a1​c2+a2​c1b1​c2−b2​c1,a1​b2+a2​b1b1​c2−b2​c1)(u^{*},v^{*}):=\biggl(\dfrac{a_{1}c_{2}+a_{2}c_{1}}{b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1}},\dfrac{a_{1}b_{2}+a_{2}b_{1}}{b_{1}c_{2}-b_{2}c_{1}}\biggr) (2.3)

provided that either of the following three conditions holds:

(i) 0<a1,a2;(ii) a2<0<a1andb1b2<a1|a2|;(iii) a1<0<a2and|a1|a2<c1c2.\begin{array}[]{rll}\text{(i) }&0<a_{1},\,a_{2};\\ \text{(ii) }&a_{2}<0<a_{1}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\dfrac{b_{1}}{b_{2}}<\dfrac{a_{1}}{|a_{2}|};\\ \text{(iii) }&a_{1}<0<a_{2}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\dfrac{|a_{1}|}{a_{2}}<\dfrac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}.\end{array} (2.4)

The next result asserts that under the same conditions as Theorem 2.1, if there is a positive constant steady state (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) and the equal random diffusion rate is sufficiently large, then (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) is globally asymptotically stable (GAS):

Theorem 2.2.

Let d1=d2(=:d)d_{1}=d_{2}\,(\,=:d\,) and Ω\Omega be a bounded convex domain in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} with N≤3N\leq 3. Assume (2.1) and either of (i)-(iii) in (2.4), Then there exists d¯=d¯​(α,β,ai,bi,ci)>0\overline{d}=\overline{d}(\alpha,\beta,a_{i},b_{i},c_{i})>0 such that if d≥d¯d\geq\overline{d}, then any positive solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) satisfies

limt→∞(u⁡(⋅,t),v⁡(⋅,t))=(u∗,v∗)inL2​(Ω)×L2​(Ω).\lim_{t\to\infty}(u(\,\cdot\,,t),v(\,\cdot\,,t))=(u^{*},v^{*})\quad\mbox{in}\quad L^{2}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega). (2.5)

Here we refer to some results on the existence of nonconstant positive steady states found by Adachi and the second author [1]. According to an interpretation of [1, Theorem 1] for the case where d1=d2(=:d)d_{1}=d_{2}\,(\,=:d) and either of (ii) or (iii) in (2.4) is imposed, if some additional conditions involving (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) are assumed, then there exists a positive sequence {d∗(j)}\{d^{(j)}_{*}\} with d∗(j)→0d^{(j)}_{*}\to 0 (j→∞)(j\to\infty) such that nonconstant positive steady states bifurcate from (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) at d=d∗(j)d=d^{(j)}_{*} (see Theorem 5.1 below in the case where (ii) of (2.4) is assumed). Then, in a range of small d>0d>0, infinitely many bifurcation points appear on the branch {(d,u∗,v∗)}\{(d,u^{*},v^{*})\} of the positive constant steady state from which nonconstant steady states bifurcate due to the effect of α\alpha and β\beta. Hence for such a small range of dd, (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) is no longer globally asymptotically stable. This scenario is totally different from that of the weak cooperative linear diffusive system with α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 in (1.1), where all positive solutions tend to (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) as t→∞t\to\infty.

3. Existence of the L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) absorbing set

This section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 2.1.

3.1. A priori estimates for w=u+γ​vw=u+\gamma v

Taking an advantage of the equal random diffusion rates, we first show the L∞​(Ω)L^{\infty}(\Omega) a priori estimate for w=u+γ​vw=u+\gamma v using the comparison theorem for a semilinear heat equation which ww satisfies.

Lemma 3.1.

Let d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and assume (2.1). For any nonnegative functions u0u_{0}, and v0v_{0} belong to W1,∞​(Ω)W^{1,\infty}(\Omega), let (u,v)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω×(0,Tmax))]2(u,v)\in[\,C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{{\rm max}}))\cap C^{2,1}(\Omega\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}))\,]^{2} be the solution of (1.1), which is ensured by Theorem 1.1. Then, there exist a positive function ξ⁡(t)\xi(t) uniformly bounded in [0,∞)[0,\infty) and a positive constant λ∗=λ∗​(bi,ci,γ)\lambda^{*}=\lambda^{*}(b_{i},c_{i},\gamma) such that ξ⁡(0)=‖u0+γ​v0‖L∞​(Ω)\xi(0)=\|u_{0}+\gamma v_{0}\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)},

w⁡(x,t):=u⁡(x,t)+γ​v​(x,t)≤ξ⁡(t)for all​(x,t)∈Ω×(0,Tmax),w(x,t):=u(x,t)+\gamma v(x,t)\leq\xi(t)\quad\mbox{for all}\ (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}),

and

limt→∞ξ⁡(t)=(1+γ2)​a~λ∗,\lim_{t\to\infty}\xi(t)=\dfrac{(1+\gamma^{2})\widetilde{a}}{\lambda^{*}},

Proof.

wt=d​Δ​w+u⁡(a1−b1​u+c1​v)+γ​v​(a2+b2​u−c2​v)=d​Δ​w+a1​u+γ​a2​v−[u,v]​[b1−c1+γ​b22−c1+γ​b22γ​c2]​[uv].\begin{split}w_{t}&=d\Delta w+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v)+\gamma v(a_{2}+b_{2}u-c_{2}v)\\ &=d\Delta w+a_{1}u+\gamma a_{2}v-[u,v]\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}b_{1}&-\frac{c_{1}+\gamma b_{2}}{2}\\ -\frac{c_{1}+\gamma b_{2}}{2}&\gamma c_{2}\end{array}\right]\left[\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ v\end{array}\right].\end{split} (3.1)

The following lemma is based on the maximal regularity theory for (3.1) and will help in the derivation of the W1,4​(Ω)W^{1,4}(\Omega) a priori estimate of uu and vv.

Lemma 3.2.

Assume d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and (2.1). 3.2. Hölder estimate

It has already been shown that uu and vv are uniformly bounded on Ω×(0,Tmax)\Omega\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}) under the assumptions of Lemma 3.1. The following lemma gives the Hölder estimate of uu and vv. This Hölder estimate will play a role of a condition for application of an Ehring-type inequality when deriving the W1,4​(Ω)W^{1,4}(\Omega) a priori estimate later.

Lemma 3.3.

Assume d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and (2.1). For nonnegative functions u0u_{0}, and v0v_{0} belonging to W1,∞​(Ω)W^{1,\infty}(\Omega), let (u,v)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))]2(u,v)\in[\,C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{{\rm max}}))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}))\,]^{2} be the solution of (1.1), which is ensured by Theorem 1.1. ∫tt+τ(‖w⁡(⋅,s)‖W2,p​(Ω)p+‖wt​(⋅,s)‖Lp​(Ω)p)​𝑑s≤C^1for all​t∈(τ,T^max)\int^{t+\tau}_{t}\left(\|w(\,\cdot\,,s)\|^{p}_{W^{2,p}(\Omega)}+\|w_{t}(\,\cdot\,,s)\|^{p}_{L^{p}(\Omega)}\right)\,ds\leq\widehat{C}_{1}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(\tau,\widehat{T}_{{\rm max}})

with some C^1>0\widehat{C}_{1}>0. By the embedding theorem [5, Theorem 5.2] with suitably large pp, one can find C~1\widetilde{C}_{1} such that

‖∇w​(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)≤C~1for all​t∈(τ,Tmax).\|\nabla w(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}\leq\widetilde{C}_{1}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(\tau,T_{{\rm max}}). (3.9)

Obviously, Lemma 3.1 yields C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} such that

u⁡(x,t)≤C1,v⁡(x,t)≤C2for all​(x,t)∈Ω×(0,Tmax).u(x,t)\leq C_{1},\quad v(x,t)\leq C_{2}\quad\mbox{for all}\ (x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}). (3.10)

In order to apply the Hölder regularity theory for a class of quasilinear parabolic equations by Porzio and Vespri [15, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.4], we note the following divergence form by substituting (1.2) and ∇v=(∇w−∇u)/γ\nabla v=(\nabla w-\nabla u)/\gamma into the first equation of (1.1):

ut=∇⋅(d∇u+αv∇u−αu∇v)+u(a1−b1u+c1v)=∇⋅(d∇u+αv∇u−βu∇w+βu∇u)+u(a1−b1u+c1v)=∇⋅{(d+βu+αv)∇u−βu∇w}+f(u,v),\begin{split}u_{t}&=\nabla\cdot(\,d\,\nabla u+\alpha v\nabla u-\alpha u\nabla v\,)+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v)\\ &=\nabla\cdot(\,d\,\nabla u+\alpha v\nabla u-\beta u\nabla w+\beta u\nabla u\,)+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v)\\ &=\nabla\cdot\{\,(\,d+\beta u+\alpha v\,)\nabla u-\beta u\nabla w\,\}+f(u,v),\end{split} (3.11)

where f⁡(u,v):=u⁡(a1−b1​u+c1​v)f(u,v):=u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v). In view of (3.11), we define an ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} valued function 𝑨⁡(x,t,ξ)\boldsymbol{A}(x,t,\xi) and a real valued function B⁡(x,t)B(x,t) as follows:

𝑨(x,t,ξ):=(d+βu(x,t)+αv(x,t))ξ−βu(x,t)∇w(x,t),(x,t,ξ)∈Ω×(0,Tmax)×ℝN,B⁡(x,t):=f⁡(u⁡(x,t),v⁡(x,t)),(x,t)∈Ω×(0,Tmax).\begin{split}\boldsymbol{A}(x,t,\xi):=(d+\beta u(x,t)+\alpha v(x,t))\xi-\beta u(x,t)\nabla w(x,t),\quad&(x,t,\xi)\in\Omega\times(0,T_{{\rm max}})\times\mathbb{R}^{N},\\ B(x,t):=f(u(x,t),v(x,t)),\quad&(x,t)\in\Omega\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}).\end{split}

ut=∇⋅𝑨⁡(x,t,∇u)+B⁡(x,t).u_{t}=\nabla\cdot\boldsymbol{A}(x,t,\nabla u)+B(x,t).

|𝑨⁡(x,t,∇u)|≤(d+β​C1+α​C2)​|∇u|+β​C1​C~1|\boldsymbol{A}(x,t,\nabla u)|\leq(d+\beta C_{1}+\alpha C_{2})|\nabla u|+\beta C_{1}\widetilde{C}_{1} (3.13)

and

|B⁡(x,t)|≤C1​(a1++c1​C2)|B(x,t)|\leq C_{1}(a_{1}^{+}+c_{1}C_{2}) (3.14)

for all (x,t)∈Ω×(τ,Tmax)(x,t)\in\Omega\times(\tau,T_{{\rm max}}). Owing to the structural conditions (3.12), (3.13) and (3.14), one can use [15, Theorem 1.3 and Remark 1.4] to find θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) and C^2\widehat{C}_{2} such that

‖u‖Cθ,θ/2​(Ω¯×[t,t+τ])≤C^2for all​t∈(τ,T^max).\|u\|_{C^{\theta,\theta/2}(\overline{\Omega}\times[t,t+\tau])}\leq\widehat{C}_{2}\qquad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(\tau,\widehat{T}_{{\rm max}}).

In the same manner, we can also get the desired Hölder estimate for vv. ∎

3.3. W1,4​(Ω)W^{1,4}(\Omega) estimate

We have seen that under the conditions d1=d2d_{1}=d_{2} and (2.1), any nonnegative solution (u,v)(u,v) of (1.1) remains bounded in the sense that ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖L∞​(Ω)\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)}+\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{\infty}(\Omega)} never blows up as t↗Tmaxt\nearrow T_{{\rm max}}. It should be noted that this fact alone does not allow us to conclude Tmax=∞T_{{\rm max}}=\infty. This is because, although the maximum values of uu and vv remain bounded as t↗Tmaxt\nearrow T_{{\rm max}}, the possibility of blowing up of any of partial derivatives of uu or vv below the second order cannot be ruled out. In view of Theorem 1.1, we recall that if Tmax<∞T_{{\rm max}}<\infty, then ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p​(Ω)\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}+\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} blows up as t↗Tmaxt\nearrow T_{{\rm max}} for any p>Np>N. Therefore, focusing on its counterpart, if it can be shown that ‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,p​(Ω)\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}+\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} remains bounded as t↗Tmaxt\nearrow T_{\rm max} with some p>Np>N, then we can conclude not only Tmax=∞T_{{\rm max}}=\infty but also what the solution (u,v)(u,v) becomes a time-global classical solution.

Therefore, in this subsection, we show the uniform W1,4​(Ω)W^{1,4}(\Omega) a priori estimate for any nonnegative solution (u,v)(u,v) with additional conditions that N≤3N\leq 3 and Ω\Omega is convex. To this end, we note a useful inequality of the Gronwall type described in [16, Lemma 3.4].

Lemma 3.4 ([16]).

Let T>0T>0 and y⁡(t)∈[0,∞)y(t)\in[0,\infty) be an absolutely continuous function for t∈[0,T)t\in[0,T) satisfying

dd​t​y​(t)+a​y​(t)≤h⁡(t)for a.e.​t∈(0,T)\dfrac{d}{dt}y(t)+ay(t)\leq h(t)\quad\mbox{for a.e.}\ t\in(0,T) (3.15)

with some a>0a>0 and a nonnegative measurable function h⁡(t)h(t) for which there exists b>0b>0 such that

∫tt+1h(s)ds≤bfor allt∈[0,T−1).\int^{t+1}_{t}h(s)\,ds\leq b\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in[0,T-1).

Then

y⁡(t)≤max⁡{y⁡(0)+b,ba+2​b}for all​t∈(0,T).y(t)\leq\max\biggl\{y(0)+b,\dfrac{b}{a}+2b\biggr\}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(0,T). (3.16)

Hereafter we derive (3.15) for y⁡(t):=‖∇u​(⋅,t)‖L4​(Ω)4+‖∇v​(⋅,t)‖L4​(Ω)4y(t):=\|\nabla u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4}+\|\nabla v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{L^{4}(\Omega)}^{4} with some h⁡(t)h(t) for the boundedness of y⁡(t)y(t) on t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{{\rm max}}) as (3.16). The proof is inspired by the idea of Lou and Winkler [12, Lemma 5.2] on the construction of time-global solutions of the Shigesada-Kawasaki-Teramoto model.

Lemma 3.5.

Let Ω\Omega be a bounded convex domain in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} with N≤3N\leq 3. Assume d1=d2(=:d)d_{1}=d_{2}\,(\,=:d) and (2.1). For nonnegative u0u_{0}, v0∈W1,∞​(Ω)v_{0}\in W^{1,\infty}(\Omega), let (u,v)∈[C⁡(Ω¯×[0,Tmax))∩C2,1​(Ω¯×(0,Tmax))]2(u,v)\in[\,C(\overline{\Omega}\times[0,T_{{\rm max}}))\cap C^{2,1}(\overline{\Omega}\times(0,T_{{\rm max}}))\,]^{2} be the solution of (1.1). Then there exists C>0C>0 such that CC is independent of t∈(0,Tmax)t\in(0,T_{{\rm max}}) and

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,4​(Ω)+‖v⁡(⋅,t)‖W1,4​(Ω)≤Cfor all​t∈(0,Tmax).\|u(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,4}(\Omega)}+\|v(\,\cdot\,,t)\|_{W^{1,4}(\Omega)}\leq C\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in(0,T_{{\rm max}}).
Proof.

In the proof, xx and the dot symbol for the spatial variable and tt for the time variable are omitted unless there is confusion. Substituting the first equation of (1.1) into

14dd​t∥∇u∥4L4​(Ω)=∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇ut,\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d}{dt}\|\nabla u\|^{4}_{L^{4}(\Omega)}=\displaystyle\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla u_{t},

we get

14dd​t∥∇u∥4L4​(Ω)−d∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇Δu=α∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇(vΔu−uΔv)+∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇f(u,v),\begin{split}&\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d}{dt}\|\nabla u\|^{4}_{L^{4}(\Omega)}-d\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla\Delta u\\ =\,&\alpha\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla f(u,v),\end{split} (3.17)

where f⁡(u,v)=u⁡(a1−b1​u+c1​v)f(u,v)=u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v). Substituting the identity

∇u⋅∇Δu=12Δ|∇u|2−|D2u|2\nabla u\cdot\nabla\Delta u=\dfrac{1}{2}\Delta|\nabla u|^{2}-|D^{2}u|^{2}

into the random diffusion term gives

−d∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇Δu=d(−12∫Ω|∇u|2Δ|∇u|2+∫Ω|∇u|2|D2u|2).-d\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla\Delta u=d\,\biggl(-\dfrac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\Delta|\nabla u|^{2}+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}|D^{2}u|^{2}\biggr).

We integrate by parts in the first term of the right-hand side to get

∫Ω|∇u|2​Δ​|∇u|2=∫∂Ω|∇u|2​∂|∇u|2∂ν−∫Ω|∇|∇u|2|2.\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\Delta|\nabla u|^{2}=\int_{\partial\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\dfrac{\partial|\nabla u|^{2}}{\partial\nu}-\int_{\Omega}|\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}|^{2}.

Since ∂|∇u|2/∂ν≤0\partial|\nabla u|^{2}/\partial\nu\leq 0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega when Ω\Omega is convex (e.g., [11, Lemma 1.1]), then

−d∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇Δu≥d∫Ω|∇u|2|D2u|2.-d\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla\Delta u\geq d\,\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}|D^{2}u|^{2}.

Then, together with integration by parts in the first term of the right-hand side of (3.17), we obtain

14dd​t∥∇u∥L4​(Ω)4+d∫Ω|∇u|2|D2u|2≤I(t)+J(t)+∫Ω|∇u|2∇u⋅∇f(u,v),\dfrac{1}{4}\dfrac{d}{dt}\|\nabla u\|^{4}_{L^{4}(\Omega)}+d\,\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}|D^{2}u|^{2}\leq I(t)+J(t)+\int_{\Omega}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla f(u,v), (3.18)

where

I:=−α∫Ω(vΔu−uΔv)|∇u|2Δu,J:=−α∫Ω(vΔu−uΔv)∇|∇u|2⋅∇u.I:=-\alpha\int_{\Omega}(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)|\nabla u|^{2}\Delta u,\qquad J:=-\alpha\int_{\Omega}(v\Delta u-u\Delta v)\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\cdot\nabla u.

Substituting Δ​v=(Δ​w−Δ​u)/γ\Delta v=(\Delta w-\Delta u)/\gamma and γ​v+u=w\gamma v+u=w into II gives

I=−β∫Ωw|∇u|2|Δu|2+β∫Ωu|∇u|2ΔuΔw.I=-\beta\int_{\Omega}w|\nabla u|^{2}|\Delta u|^{2}+\beta\int_{\Omega}u|\nabla u|^{2}\Delta u\Delta w. (3.19)

Substituting Δ​v=(Δ​w−Δ​u)/γ\Delta v=(\Delta w-\Delta u)/\gamma into JJ gives

J=∫Ω(−αvΔu+βuΔw−βuΔu)∇|∇u|2⋅∇u.J=\int_{\Omega}(-\alpha v\Delta u+\beta u\Delta w-\beta u\Delta u)\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\cdot\nabla u.

Owing to the facts that ∂|∇u|2/∂ν≤0\partial|\nabla u|^{2}/\partial\nu\leq 0 on ∂Ω\partial\Omega and ∇Δu⋅∇u=12Δ|∇u|2−|D2u|2\nabla\Delta u\cdot\nabla u=\frac{1}{2}\Delta|\nabla u|^{2}-|D^{2}u|^{2}, straight forward calculations using integration by parts lead to

J≤α∫Ω(v|∇u|2|Δu|2+|∇u|2(∇u⋅∇v)Δu−12|∇u|2∇v⋅∇|∇u|2)+β∫ΩuΔw∇|∇u|2⋅∇u+β∫Ω(u|∇u|2|Δu|2+|∇u|4Δu−12|∇u|2∇u⋅∇|∇u|2).\begin{split}J&\leq\,\alpha\int_{\Omega}\,\biggl(\,v|\nabla u|^{2}|\Delta u|^{2}+|\nabla u|^{2}(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v)\Delta u-\dfrac{1}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla v\cdot\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\,\biggr)\\ &+\beta\int_{\Omega}u\Delta w\,\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\cdot\nabla u\\ &+\beta\int_{\Omega}\biggl(\,u|\nabla u|^{2}|\Delta u|^{2}+|\nabla u|^{4}\Delta u-\dfrac{1}{2}|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\,\biggr).\end{split}

Since β​u+α​v=β​w\beta u+\alpha v=\beta w, we see

J≤β∫Ωw|∇u|2|Δu|2+α∫Ω(|∇u|2(∇u⋅∇v)Δu−12|∇u|2∇v⋅∇|∇u|2)+β∫Ω(uΔw∇|∇u|2⋅∇u+|∇u|4Δu−12|∇u|2∇u⋅∇|∇u|2).\begin{split}J&\leq\beta\int_{\Omega}w|\nabla u|^{2}|\Delta u|^{2}+\alpha\int_{\Omega}\biggl(|\nabla u|^{2}(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v)\Delta u-\dfrac{1}{2}\,|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla v\cdot\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\biggr)\\ &+\beta\int_{\Omega}\biggl(u\Delta w\,\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\cdot\nabla u+|\nabla u|^{4}\Delta u-\dfrac{1}{2}\,|\nabla u|^{2}\nabla u\cdot\nabla|\nabla u|^{2}\biggr).\end{split} (3.20)

Adding (3.19) and (3.20) cancels each other’s first terms in the right-hand sides and results in

4. Global asymptotic stability of the positive constant steady state

In this section, we give a proof of Theorem 2.2. In order to show the global asymptotic stability of the positive constant steady state (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) stated as (2.5), we construct a Lyapunov function. To do so, we introduce a nonnegative function H⁡(η,ξ)H(\eta;\xi) as follows:

Under the assumptions of Theorem 2.2, let (u,v)(u,v) be the positive solution of (1.1) (which exists globally in time by Theorem 2.1). Therefore, for the above ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists δ>0\delta>0 such that

|t−tn|<δ⟹|𝒟⁡(t)−𝒟⁡(tn)|<ε2for all​t∈[t0,∞)andn∈ℕ.|t-t_{n}|<\delta\ \Longrightarrow\ |\mathcal{D}(t)-\mathcal{D}(t_{n})|<\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\quad\mbox{for all}\ t\in[t_{0},\infty)\quad\mbox{and}\quad n\in\mathbb{N}.

Then it follows that

𝒟⁡(t)≥𝒟⁡(tn)−|𝒟⁡(tn)−𝒟⁡(t)|≥ε−ε2=ε2\mathcal{D}(t)\geq\mathcal{D}(t_{n})-|\mathcal{D}(t_{n})-\mathcal{D}(t)|\geq\varepsilon-\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}=\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}

if t∈(tn,tn+δ)t\in(t_{n},t_{n}+\delta) with each n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Therefore, we know that

∫tntn+δ𝒟⁡(t)​𝑑t≥∫tntn+δε2​𝑑t=δ​ε2>0for all​n∈ℕ,\int^{t_{n}+\delta}_{t_{n}}\mathcal{D}(t)\,dt\geq\int^{t_{n}+\delta}_{t_{n}}\dfrac{\varepsilon}{2}\,dt=\dfrac{\delta\varepsilon}{2}>0\quad\mbox{for all}\ n\in\mathbb{N},

whereas (4.6) obviously leads to

∫tntn+δ𝒟⁡(t)​𝑑t→0as​n→∞.\int^{t_{n}+\delta}_{t_{n}}\mathcal{D}(t)\,dt\to 0\quad\mbox{as}\ n\to\infty.

This contradiction enables us to conclude that 𝒟⁡(t)→0\mathcal{D}(t)\to 0 as t→∞t\to\infty, namely,

limt→∞(u⁡(⋅,t),v⁡(⋅,t))=(u∗,v∗)in​L2​(Ω)×L2​(Ω).\lim_{t\to\infty}(u(\,\cdot\,,t),v(\,\cdot\,,t))=(u^{*},v^{*})\quad\mbox{in}\ L^{2}(\Omega)\times L^{2}(\Omega).

Then we complete the proof of Theorem 2.2. ∎

5. Relationship between stationary and nonstationary solutions

In this section, we discuss the relationship between the bifurcation structure of the nonconstant positive steady states obtained in [1] and the time-global nonstationary solutions obtained up to the previous section. In [1], Adachi and the second author of the present paper studied the corresponding stationary problem in the weak cooperative case b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}. Among other things, they showed that nonconstant positive steady states bifurcate from the positive constant steady state (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) when either of (ii) or (iii) of (2.4) (under b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}) is satisfied in addition to some conditions. In [1], did_{i} (i=1​or​ 2)(i=1\ \mbox{or}\ 2) is adopted as the bifurcation parameter, but in order to relate the results of [1] to the properties of the nonstationary solutions of (1.1) obtained up to the previous section, we state the results of [1] for the stationary problem with equal random diffusion rates.

{dΔu+α∇⋅[v2∇(uv)]+u(a1−b1u+c1v)=0,x∈Ω,dΔv+β∇⋅[u2∇(vu)]+v(a2+b2u−c2v)=0,x∈Ω,∂u∂ν=∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω\begin{cases}d\Delta u+\alpha\nabla\cdot\biggl[v^{2}\,\nabla\biggl(\dfrac{u}{v}\biggr)\biggr]+u(a_{1}-b_{1}u+c_{1}v)=0,\ \ \ &x\in\Omega,\\ d\Delta v+\beta\nabla\cdot\biggl[u^{2}\,\nabla\biggl(\dfrac{v}{u}\biggr)\biggr]+v(a_{2}+b_{2}u-c_{2}v)=0,\ \ \ &x\in\Omega,\\ \dfrac{\partial u}{\partial\nu}=\dfrac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,\ \ \ &x\in\partial\Omega\end{cases} (5.1)

with bifurcation parameter dd, as Theorem 5.1 below. Since results in cases (ii) and (iii) of (2.4) can be described similarly, the result in case (ii) will be discussed. In the bifurcation structure, the eigenvalue problem:

−Δ​ϕ=λ​ϕin​Ω,∂ϕ∂ν=0on​∂Ω-\Delta\phi=\lambda\phi\quad\mbox{in}\ \Omega,\qquad\dfrac{\partial\phi}{\partial\nu}=0\quad\mbox{on}\ \partial\Omega (5.2)

will play an important role. We denote all the eigenvalues by

0=λ0<λ1≤λ2≤⋯≤λj≤⋯0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{j}\leq\cdots

counting multiplicity and denote by Φj\varPhi_{j} any L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) normalized eigenfunciton corresponding to the eigenvalue λj\lambda_{j}.

Theorem 5.1 ([1]).

Assume that

a2<0<a1,c1c2<b1b2<a1|a2|a_{2}<0<a_{1},\quad\dfrac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}<\dfrac{b_{1}}{b_{2}}<\dfrac{a_{1}}{|a_{2}|} (5.3)

and

Pj​(α,β):=λj​(α​|a2|​v∗−β​a1​u∗)−(a1​c2−|a2|​c1)​v∗>0P_{j}(\alpha,\beta):=\lambda_{j}(\alpha|a_{2}|v^{*}-\beta a_{1}u^{*})-(a_{1}c_{2}-|a_{2}|c_{1})v^{*}>0

for some j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}. If λj\lambda_{j} is a simple eigenvalue, then the curve of nonconstant solutions of (5.1) bifurcates from (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) at

d=d∗(j)​(α,β):=12​λj​(Qj2+4​Pj−Qj),d=d^{(j)}_{*}(\alpha,\beta):=\dfrac{1}{2\lambda_{j}}\left(\sqrt{Q_{j}^{2}+4P_{j}}-Q_{j}\right), (5.4)

where Qj​(α,β):=λj​(β​u∗+α​v∗)+b1​u∗+c1​v∗Q_{j}(\alpha,\beta):=\lambda_{j}(\beta u^{*}+\alpha v^{*})+b_{1}u^{*}+c_{1}v^{*}. There exist a neighborhood 𝒰j⊂ℝ×Wν2,p​(Ω)2\mathcal{U}_{j}\subset\mathbb{R}\times W^{2,p}_{\nu}(\Omega)^{2} of (d∗(j),u∗,v∗)(d^{(j)}_{*},u^{*},v^{*}) and a small positive number δj\delta_{j} such that all solutions of (5.1) (treating dd as a positive parameter) contained in 𝒰j\mathcal{U}_{j} consist of the union of {(d,u∗,v∗)∈𝒰j}\{(d,u^{*},v^{*})\in\mathcal{U}_{j}\} and a simple curve

Γj:[duv]=[d∗(j)​(α,β)u∗v∗]+[q⁡(s)s​(Φj+u~​(s))s⁡(κj​Φj+v~​(s))]for​s∈(−δj,δj)\varGamma_{j}\,:\,\left[\begin{array}[]{c}d\\ u\\ v\end{array}\right]=\left[\begin{array}[]{l}d^{(j)}_{*}(\alpha,\beta)\\ u^{*}\\ v^{*}\end{array}\right]+\left[\begin{array}[]{l}q(s)\\ s(\varPhi_{j}+\widetilde{u}(s))\\ s(\kappa_{j}\varPhi_{j}+\widetilde{v}(s))\\ \end{array}\right]\quad\mbox{for}\ s\in(-\delta_{j},\delta_{j}) (5.5)

with some κj>0\kappa_{j}>0, where (q⁡(s),u~​(s),v~​(s))∈ℝ×Wν2,p​(Ω)2(q(s),\widetilde{u}(s),\widetilde{v}(s))\in\mathbb{R}\times W^{2,p}_{\nu}(\Omega)^{2} is continuously differentiable for s∈(−δj,δj)s\in(-\delta_{j},\delta_{j}) with (q⁡(0),u~​(0),v~​(0))=(0,0,0)(q(0),\widetilde{u}(0),\widetilde{v}(0))=(0,0,0) and ∫ΩΦj​u~​(s)=∫ΩΦj​v~​(s)=0\int_{\Omega}\varPhi_{j}\widetilde{u}(s)=\int_{\Omega}\varPhi_{j}\widetilde{v}(s)=0 for s∈(−δj,δj)s\in(-\delta_{j},\delta_{j}).

From the viewpoint of the effect of the strongly coupled diffusion terms on the bifurcation structure, one can see that if

(α,β)∈⋃j=1∞ℛj,whereℛj:={(α,β)∈ℝ>02:Pj​(α,β)>0},(\alpha,\beta)\in\bigcup^{\infty}_{j=1}\mathcal{R}_{j},\quad\mbox{where}\ \ \mathcal{R}_{j}:=\{\,(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{>0}\,:\,P_{j}(\alpha,\beta)>0\,\},

then there appear infinitely many bifurcation points (d∗(j),u∗,v∗)(d_{*}^{(j)},u^{*},v^{*}) with

j≥k:=min⁡{j∈ℕ:(α,β)∈ℛj}j\geq k:=\min\{\,j\in\mathbb{N}\,:\,(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal{R}_{j}\,\}

such that λj\lambda_{j} is a simple eigenvalue of (5.2). Indeed, it is possible to check that ℛj\mathcal{R}_{j} expands to the positive cone below the line

γ=A​τ∗,whereA=a1|a2|,τ∗=u∗v∗,\gamma=A\tau^{*},\qquad\mbox{where}\ \ A=\dfrac{a_{1}}{|a_{2}|},\quad\tau^{*}=\dfrac{u^{*}}{v^{*}},

as j→∞j\to\infty on the α​β\alpha\beta plane (see Figure 1). Furthermore, from (5.4), one can verify that d∗(j)​(α,β)→0d^{(j)}_{*}(\alpha,\beta)\to 0 as j→∞j\to\infty if (α,β)∈∪j=1∞ℛj(\alpha,\beta)\in\cup^{\infty}_{j=1}\mathcal{R}_{j}. This fact implies that (α,β)∈∪j=1∞ℛj(\alpha,\beta)\in\cup^{\infty}_{j=1}\mathcal{R}_{j} can produce various stationary patterns when equal random diffusion dd is small enough. In Figure 2, when (a1,a2,b1,b2,c1,c2)=(1,−1,4,5,2,3)(a_{1},a_{2},b_{1},b_{2},c_{1},c_{2})=(1,-1,4,5,2,3) and (α,β)=(2,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(2,1), the numerical bifurcation diagram by the continuation software pde2path ([17]) is exhibited, where the horizontal axis represents dd, and the vertical axis represents ‖u‖L2​(Ω)\|u\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)} (with s∈(0,δj)s\in(0,\delta_{j}) in (5.5)). The bifurcation point d∗(j)d_{*}^{(j)} and the bifurcation branches Γj\varGamma_{j} of Theorem 5.1 can be observed within the numerically traceable range.

According to [1], in the nonlinear diffusion limit where α\alpha and β\beta tend to infinity keeping (α,β)∈∪j=1∞ℛj(\alpha,\beta)\in\cup^{\infty}_{j=1}\mathcal{R}_{j}, the positive steady states approach a positive steady state to the scalar field equation as follows:

Theorem 5.2 ([1]).

Assume (5.3) and N≤3N\leq 3. Let {(αn,βn)}\{(\alpha_{n},\beta_{n})\} be any positive sequence satisfying αn→∞\alpha_{n}\to\infty, βn→∞\beta_{n}\to\infty and αn/βn→γ\alpha_{n}/\beta_{n}\to\gamma with some γ>A​τ∗\gamma>A\tau^{*}. Let {(un,vn)}\{(u_{n},v_{n})\} be any sequence of positive nonconstant solutions of (5.1) with (α,β)=(αn,βn)(\alpha,\beta)=(\alpha_{n},\beta_{n}). Then there exists a positive function v∈C2​(Ω¯)v\in C^{2}(\overline{\Omega}) such that

limn→∞(un,vn)=(τ∗,1)​vin​C1​(Ω¯)×C1​(Ω¯),\lim_{n\to\infty}(u_{n},v_{n})=(\tau^{*},1)v\quad\mbox{in}\ C^{1}(\overline{\Omega})\times C^{1}(\overline{\Omega}),

passing to a subsequence if necessary. Furthermore, vv satisfies

{dΔv+ξ∗v(v−v∗)=0,x∈Ω,∂v∂ν=0,x∈∂Ω,\begin{cases}d\Delta v+\xi^{*}v(v-v^{*})=0,\qquad&x\in\Omega,\\ \dfrac{\partial v}{\partial\nu}=0,\qquad&x\in\partial\Omega,\end{cases} (5.6)

where

ξ∗=γ​|a2|−τ∗​a1u∗+γ​v∗.\xi^{*}=\dfrac{\gamma|a_{2}|-\tau^{*}a_{1}}{u^{*}+\gamma v^{*}}.

It is well-known that the set of positive solutions to the stationary scalar field equation such as (5.6) with small d>0d>0 is very complicated from various viewpoints, e.g. multiplicity, profiles and the bifurcation structure. Naturally it can be expected that the spatio-temporal structure of (1.1) with small equal random diffusion rates and the weak cooperative setting is very rich from the dynamical viewpoint involving the bifurcation theory, such a complicated dynamical picture of the strongly coupled diffusion system is in stark contrast with that of the weak cooperative linear diffusion system (α=β=0\alpha=\beta=0 and b1​c2>b2​c1b_{1}c_{2}>b_{2}c_{1}), where (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) is globally asymptotically stable attracting all the positive nonstationary solutions as t→∞t\to\infty regardless of the degree of the random diffusion rates.

Here in view of Theorem 2.2, we recall that if the equal random diffusion dd is sufficiently large, then all positive solutions of (1.1) with the weak cooperative setting tend to (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}) as t→∞t\to\infty. This scenario is same to the weak cooperative linear diffusion system. Consequently, for the global dynamics of the weakly cooperative strongly coupled diffusion system (1.1), we find that if the equal random diffusion dd is sufficiently large, all positive nonstationary solutions asymptotically approach (u∗,v∗)(u^{*},v^{*}), as is the case for the corresponding linear diffusion system, whereas if dd is sufficiently small, a variety of dynamics can be expected where a lot of positive nonconstant steady states exist.
